title: Understanding Quadrilaterals
prerequisites: Basic idea of angles, lines, and triangles (angle sum property of a triangle = 180°).
Familiarity with terms like parallel lines, perpendicular lines, and diagonals.
Concept of a polygon as a closed figure made of line segments.

topics.title: Polygons — Classification & Angle Sum Property
topics.quick_summary: A polygon is a closed plane figure made of straight line segments; polygons are classified by their number of sides, and the sum of their interior/exterior angles follows fixed formulas.

detailed.definition: A polygon is a simple closed figure formed by three or more line segments (sides); it is 'convex' if all interior angles are less than 180°, and 'concave' if at least one interior angle is greater than 180°.
detailed.key_idea: The sum of interior angles of a polygon depends only on its number of sides (n), given by (n−2) × 180°; the sum of exterior angles of any convex polygon is always 360°, regardless of the number of sides.
detailed.working_principle: Any polygon with n sides can be split into (n−2) triangles by drawing diagonals from one vertex; since each triangle's angles sum to 180°, the polygon's interior angle sum becomes (n−2) × 180°.
applications: Architectural and tiling designs rely on knowing which regular polygons can fit together without gaps (e.g., hexagons, squares, triangles).
Finding unknown angles in geometry problems involving multi-sided figures.

topics.real_life: A honeycomb's hexagonal cells and a stop sign's octagonal shape are real-world regular polygons, chosen partly because of how their angles fit together efficiently.
points: Sum of interior angles of a polygon with n sides = (n−2) × 180°.
Sum of exterior angles of ANY convex polygon = 360°, always.
For a regular polygon (all sides and angles equal), each interior angle = [(n−2) × 180°] / n.
A quadrilateral (n = 4) has interior angle sum = 360°.
mistakes: Using the interior angle sum formula for exterior angles (exterior angle sum is always 360°, not dependent on n).
Forgetting that the (n−2) × 180° formula only applies to simple polygons (non-self-intersecting).
Miscounting the number of sides when the polygon is irregularly drawn.
topics.memory_hook: 'Interior grows with sides, Exterior always 360' — (n−2)×180° for interior, but exterior angles always add to one full circle.
topics.advanced: The fact that exterior angles always sum to 360° regardless of the number of sides can be understood by imagining walking around the polygon's boundary: turning through each exterior angle in turn, you make exactly one full 360° rotation by the time you return to your starting direction.

topics.title: Properties of Quadrilaterals — Parallelogram & Trapezium
topics.quick_summary: A parallelogram has both pairs of opposite sides parallel and equal, with diagonals that bisect each other; a trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides.

detailed.definition: A parallelogram is a quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel. A trapezium is a quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides (called the parallel sides or bases).
detailed.key_idea: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal, opposite angles are equal, consecutive (adjacent) angles are supplementary (sum to 180°), and the diagonals bisect each other.
detailed.working_principle: These properties can be proven using congruent triangles formed by a diagonal of the parallelogram; because alternate interior angles are equal (parallel sides cut by the diagonal as a transversal), the two triangles formed are always congruent.
applications: Engineering linkages and folding mechanisms (like scissor lifts) use parallelogram properties to maintain parallel motion.
Land surveying and architectural floor plans often use trapezium-shaped plots, requiring these angle and side properties.

topics.real_life: A sliding door track (parallelogram linkage) and a trapezium-shaped table top are common real-life shapes that rely on these specific quadrilateral properties.
points: Parallelogram: opposite sides equal & parallel; opposite angles equal; diagonals bisect each other.
Sum of any two adjacent (consecutive) angles in a parallelogram = 180° (co-interior angles).
Trapezium: only ONE pair of sides is parallel; the non-parallel sides are called 'legs'.
A trapezium is 'isosceles' if its non-parallel sides (legs) are equal — then base angles are also equal.
mistakes: Assuming a trapezium has both pairs of sides parallel — only one pair is parallel by definition.
Thinking diagonals of a parallelogram are always equal — they are equal only in a rectangle (a special parallelogram).
Confusing 'opposite angles equal' with 'adjacent angles equal' in a parallelogram — adjacent angles are supplementary, not equal (unless it's a rectangle).
topics.memory_hook: 'Parallelogram: opposite twins, diagonals share the middle' — sides and angles come in equal opposite pairs, diagonals cut each other in half.
topics.advanced: Every property of a parallelogram can be derived from just two facts — opposite sides are parallel — using alternate angle theorems and triangle congruence; this is a good example of how a minimal set of definitions can generate a rich set of derived properties in geometry.

topics.title: Special Parallelograms — Rhombus, Rectangle, Square & Kite
topics.quick_summary: Rhombus, rectangle, and square are special parallelograms with extra conditions on sides, angles, or diagonals; a kite is a distinct quadrilateral with two pairs of adjacent (not opposite) equal sides.

detailed.definition: A rhombus is a parallelogram with all four sides equal; a rectangle is a parallelogram with all angles equal to 90°; a square is a parallelogram that is both a rhombus and a rectangle. A kite has two distinct pairs of adjacent equal sides but is generally NOT a parallelogram.
detailed.key_idea: Diagonals behave differently in each special quadrilateral: a rhombus's diagonals bisect each other at 90° (perpendicular bisectors); a rectangle's diagonals are equal and bisect each other; a square's diagonals are equal, perpendicular, AND bisect each other; a kite's diagonals are perpendicular but only one diagonal is bisected by the other.
detailed.working_principle: Since a square satisfies both the rhombus condition (equal sides) and the rectangle condition (equal angles), it automatically inherits diagonal properties from both — equal, perpendicular, and bisecting each other.
applications: Rhombus-shaped patterns are common in tile flooring and traditional textile/rangoli designs.
Rectangular and square shapes dominate construction (rooms, windows, screens) because right angles simplify building and fitting objects.

topics.real_life: A cricket pitch or a door is rectangular (equal diagonals, right angles); traditional kite toys give the quadrilateral 'kite' its name, with two pairs of adjacent equal sides.
points: Rhombus: all sides equal; diagonals bisect each other at right angles (perpendicular bisectors), but are not necessarily equal.
Rectangle: all angles = 90°; diagonals are equal and bisect each other, but not necessarily perpendicular.
Square: all sides equal AND all angles = 90°; diagonals equal, perpendicular, and bisect each other.
Kite: two pairs of adjacent equal sides; diagonals are perpendicular, and only the diagonal between the unequal-side vertices is bisected.
mistakes: Assuming every rhombus is a square — a rhombus only needs equal sides, not right angles.
Assuming every rectangle is a square — a rectangle only needs right angles, not equal sides.
Applying parallelogram diagonal-bisecting properties to a kite — in a kite, only ONE diagonal is bisected, not both.
topics.memory_hook: 'Square = Rhombus + Rectangle' — it inherits equal sides from the rhombus and right angles from the rectangle.
topics.advanced: This chapter builds a natural hierarchy: parallelogram ⊃ rhombus/rectangle ⊃ square — every square is a rhombus AND a rectangle AND a parallelogram, but the reverse is not true, an important distinction tested frequently through 'always/sometimes/never true' style questions.
